red.focus: Explain why law must be dependable but capable of correcting injustice.
red.summary: People need stable rules to plan their lives, and social conditions can reveal that an old rule is harmful or inadequate. Learn to distinguish changing a legal rule from applying the existing rule to new facts.
checklist: I can identify a benefit of stable precedent
I can recognize a reason a rule may need reform
I can distinguish lawful change from an official's unsupported preference

sections.title: Stability makes promises meaningful
sections.body_md: A family buys a house relying on settled property rules. If a court suddenly changes those rules without lawful justification, the family may lose security despite having acted responsibly. Stability lets people plan, invest, and organize relationships. In many legal systems, precedent and statutory continuity support that expectation. Yet a stable rule is not automatically a fair rule. Lawyers should ask both what the rule currently requires and whether its continued operation causes a legally significant problem.

Lawyers should ask both what the rule currently requires and whether its continued operation causes a legally significant problem.

sections.title: New realities can expose old gaps
sections.body_md: A statute enacted before widespread digital communication may still protect private correspondence, but its language may leave questions about cloud storage. A court must interpret existing law through its recognized method; a legislature may decide to amend it. Those are different institutional acts. Innovation does not give every official a power to replace law by personal preference. A good student identifies the new factual problem, the present legal source, and the body permitted to make an enduring change.

A good student identifies the new factual problem, the present legal source, and the body permitted to make an enduring change.

sections.title: Change should be understandable
sections.body_md: Suppose a school policy that once seemed neutral is found to exclude a group of children unjustifiably. Reform can serve equality, but affected families and officials need notice, transition arrangements, and reasons explaining the new rule. Not every correction can avoid disruption, especially where basic rights are at stake. The goal is lawful evolution that protects people rather than surprise decision-making. A beginning lawyer should be able to explain what changed, who authorized it, and when it takes effect.

yellow.focus: Analyze stare decisis and the legitimate grounds for overruling precedent.
yellow.summary: Precedent promotes consistency and reliance, yet courts sometimes depart from earlier holdings. Learn to distinguish binding precedent, factual distinction, overruling, and legislative amendment.
checklist: I can state the purpose of stare decisis
I can distinguish overruling from distinguishing a case
I can explain reliance and workability as considerations in change

sections.title: Precedent connects cases through time
sections.body_md: Stare decisis expresses the practice of respecting authoritative prior decisions within the applicable judicial hierarchy. It promotes equality between similar cases and makes the law easier to anticipate. Its force varies by legal system and by the court considering departure. A lower court generally cannot disregard binding authority merely because the judge would decide differently. A student must identify the actual holding, not every sentence in a judgment, before claiming that precedent controls a later dispute.
sections.audio_script: Stare decisis expresses the practice of respecting authoritative prior decisions within the applicable judicial hierarchy. It promotes equality between similar cases and makes the law easier to anticipate. Its force varies by legal system and by the court considering departure. A lower court generally cannot disregard binding authority merely because the judge would decide differently. A student must identify the actual holding, not every sentence in a judgment, before claiming that precedent controls a later dispute.

sections.title: Distinguishing is not overruling
sections.body_md: A court distinguishes a case when a material difference makes its rule inapplicable; overruling rejects a previously authoritative legal proposition. A statute may change the governing law through a different institutional process. These possibilities cannot be treated as synonyms. For example, a precedent about an ordinary traffic stop may not govern a materially different search of a home under the same constitutional framework. The lawyer should explain the factual or doctrinal distinction before asking a court to abandon a stable rule.
sections.audio_script: A court distinguishes a case when a material difference makes its rule inapplicable; overruling rejects a previously authoritative legal proposition. A statute may change the governing law through a different institutional process. These possibilities cannot be treated as synonyms. For example, a precedent about an ordinary traffic stop may not govern a materially different search of a home under the same constitutional framework. The lawyer should explain the factual or doctrinal distinction before asking a court to abandon a stable rule.

sections.title: Reconsideration needs serious reasons
sections.body_md: A court with power to overrule may consider the earlier rule's reasoning, its practical workability, legal developments, reliance interests, and compatibility with binding sources. The relevant factors differ among jurisdictions and contexts. A rule can be widely relied upon yet perpetuate unlawful exclusion; correcting it may still be necessary. A carefully reasoned judgment acknowledges those costs and explains whether relief applies retrospectively or prospectively under the law. Legal change is a responsibility to those who relied on the old arrangement and those harmed by it.

orange.focus: Explain constitutional adaptation through Brown and competing interpretive approaches.
orange.summary: Constitutional texts endure while social practices and legal understandings change. Compare historical meaning, precedential development, and principles that can correct entrenched injustice.
checklist: I can explain how Brown changed the treatment of school segregation
I can distinguish originalist and living-constitution arguments without caricature
I can assess a role for reliance when a precedent protects discrimination

sections.title: Brown illustrates justified disruption
sections.body_md: Plessy v Ferguson accepted separate-but-equal reasoning in a railway context in 1896. Brown v Board of Education held state-imposed racial segregation of public schools unconstitutional in 1954, rejecting that approach in education. The judgment did not instantly remove every barrier, and subsequent remedies and resistance complicated implementation. Its importance to the stability debate is direct: reliance on discriminatory systems does not automatically justify preserving them. A court still owes a reasoned legal account of why its reading of constitutional equality governs.

Its importance to the stability debate is direct: reliance on discriminatory systems does not automatically justify preserving them. A court still owes a reasoned legal account of why its reading of constitutional equality governs.

sections.title: Interpretive theories differ over change
sections.body_md: Originalist approaches emphasize the Constitution's original public meaning, though originalists disagree about how general principles apply to modern facts. Living-constitution approaches emphasize doctrinal and principled development in light of changed circumstances, while remaining subject to debates over constraint. Neither school can accurately be reduced to 'never change' or 'let judges decide anything.' A serious comparison names the authoritative text, historical record, relevant precedent, institutional role, and what kinds of change the theory permits.

A serious comparison names the authoritative text, historical record, relevant precedent, institutional role, and what kinds of change the theory permits.

sections.title: Reliance is not the only value
sections.body_md: A public institution may have organized a longstanding practice around a precedent, while affected citizens have endured continuing exclusion. Courts must decide which reliance interests deserve legal weight and how rights violations should be remedied. An advanced analysis examines legal justification, procedural posture, administrative transition, and the persons whose interests have historically been ignored. The proper balance depends on binding doctrine. But intellectual honesty requires naming that a familiar practice may be both stable and unjust, and that correcting it can carry costs.

black.focus: Defend legal continuity while protecting constitutional correction and democratic reform.
black.summary: Stability promotes equality under law but may institutionalize historical domination; rapid doctrinal change can vindicate rights but jeopardize democratic planning. Develop a legitimate mechanism for precedent, amendment, and transition.
checklist: I can critique reliance claims that perpetuate domination
I can compare judicial revision with democratic amendment
I can design transparent transitions that protect rights without arbitrary surprise

sections.title: Stability has a distributional dimension
sections.body_md: A corporation may invoke reliance on a rule that allowed conduct imposing hidden costs on vulnerable people. Those harmed might have relied on the promise of constitutional equality rather than the existing unlawful practice. A theory of precedent should not count only the expectations of powerful institutions. Identify the legal force of both interests, evidence of dependence, and possibility of tailored transition. A doctoral analysis should reject both automatic preservation and automatic overthrow as substitutes for a careful justification of public legal authority.

A theory of precedent should not count only the expectations of powerful institutions. Identify the legal force of both interests, evidence of dependence, and possibility of tailored transition. A doctoral analysis should reject both automatic preservation and automatic overthrow as substitutes for a careful justification of public legal authority.

sections.title: The institution making change matters
sections.body_md: A legislature can enact reforms prospectively, subject to constitutional limits and political processes. Courts interpret and sometimes overrule existing precedent within their lawful competence. Constitutional amendment may require a specially demanding procedure. These routes differ in transparency, democratic participation, speed, and protection of entrenched rights. A legal system should not rely exclusively on either judicial creativity or legislative inertia. Justified change depends on the issue's source, the institution entitled to act, and the correction available when that institution errs.

sections.title: Build accountable doctrinal evolution
sections.body_md: Propose public reasons for overruling, explicit analysis of rights and reliance, predictable implementation rules, and continued review of effects. Where severe constitutional injustice persists, explain when immediate relief must outweigh administrative reliance. Where ordinary economic regulation changes, consider lawful notice and transition periods. Separate present doctrine from your preferred framework. The deepest question is not whether law should stay still or move; it is how law can remain a source of trustworthy reasons while admitting its own mistakes and correcting them.
